title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's)
directAnswer: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum. Brute force checks every subarray in O(n²). Kadane's algorithm does it in one pass: keep a running sum, and whenever that running sum goes negative, drop it and start fresh from the current element — because a negative prefix can only drag down whatever comes next. Track the best running sum seen along the way.

remember.pattern: Kadane's — running sum with negative-prefix reset
remember.formula:
cur = max(num, cur + num)   # extend, or start fresh at num
best = max(best, cur)
# init: cur = best = nums[0]
rules: Carry a **running sum** `cur`; at each element choose `max(num, cur + num)` — extend the previous subarray or restart at `num`.
You restart precisely when **`cur + num < num`**, i.e. when the previous `cur` was negative — a negative prefix only hurts.
Track `best` **separately** from `cur`; the running sum dips and resets, but `best` only ever climbs.
Initialise both to `nums[0]`, not 0 — an all-negative array must return its largest (least negative) element, and 0 would be wrong.
It's **DP and greedy at once**: `cur` is 'best subarray *ending here*' (DP state), and discarding a negative prefix is the greedy local choice that's provably global.
whenToUse: Maximum / minimum sum (or product) of a *contiguous* subarray or substring window
A running accumulator where a negative (or otherwise harmful) prefix should be discarded
One-pass, O(1)-space optimisation over an obvious O(n²) subarray scan
'Best ending here' can be computed from 'best ending at the previous index' in O(1)
antiSignals: Subarray need not be contiguous → it's a subsequence/knapsack problem, not Kadane's
You need the indices of *all* maximal subarrays → augment, or use a different scan
Elements can be reordered → sorting/greedy on values, contiguity no longer matters
Products with negatives flip signs → track both max and min (Maximum Product Subarray)
remember.takeaway: Kadane's is the canonical 'best-ending-here' scan: one running value, reset it the instant it stops helping, and remember the best you ever saw. The same shape — local DP state plus a greedy discard — reappears in Best Time to Buy/Sell Stock, Maximum Product Subarray, and Maximum Sum Circular Subarray.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can move from the brute-force O(n²) subarray scan to the O(n) one-pass insight — and articulate *why* dropping a negative running prefix is always safe (the greedy/DP justification), not just memorise the two-liner.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Initialising the running and best sums to 0, which returns 0 on an all-negative array like [-3,-1,-2] instead of the correct -1; or comparing/resetting in the wrong order so a fresh start is missed.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain Kadane's as the duality of DP ('best subarray ending at i') and greedy ('discard a negative prefix'), handle the all-negative edge case explicitly, and mention the Divide & Conquer O(n log n) variant exists for the follow-up.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the ***contiguous*** subarray (containing at least one number) which has the **largest sum**, and return its sum.

A **subarray** is a contiguous part of an array.
constraints: The subarray must contain at least one element
Elements may be negative, zero, or positive
understanding: Among all contiguous slices of the array, find the one whose elements add up to the most. The slice must be non-empty and unbroken — you can't skip elements in the middle. With negatives in play, the trick is knowing when to abandon a losing run.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the subarray have to be contiguous?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole problem. If gaps were allowed you'd just sum all the positives; contiguity is what makes the running-sum reset necessary.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be all negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. [-3, -1, -2] must return -1, the largest single element. This is why you can't initialise the answer to 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is an empty subarray allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — at least one element. So even an all-negative array has an answer (its max element), never 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to return the subarray itself or just the sum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the sum for LeetCode 53. Returning the indices is a common follow-up — track the start/end as you reset.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach

approaches.name: Brute Force — Sum Every Subarray
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the O(n²) baseline, then pivot to 'we can avoid recomputing sums by carrying a running total' — that transition leads straight to Kadane's.
hints: A subarray is fixed by its start and end index. How many (start, end) pairs are there, and how would you score each?
Fix a start i, then extend the end j rightward, maintaining a running sum so you don't re-add from scratch each time.
Track a global best across all (i, j). That's two nested loops with an O(1) running sum inside — O(n²) total.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are about n²/2 subarrays; by carrying a running sum in the inner loop we score each in O(1), so the work is O(n²) time and O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Enumerate every contiguous subarray and keep the largest sum. Fix a start index `i`, then sweep an end index `j` from `i` to the end, accumulating `nums[j]` into a running total and comparing it against the global best.

**Why carry a running sum instead of re-summing.** A naive triple loop (recomputing each subarray's sum from scratch) is O(n³). By keeping a `sum` that we extend as `j` advances, scoring each subarray costs O(1) and the whole thing drops to O(n²). It's worth saying this out loud — it shows you optimise inside a loop before throwing the whole approach away.

**Why this is the honest first answer.** It directly encodes the definition: 'try all contiguous subarrays, take the max'. It's obviously correct and a good warm-up to reason about, which is exactly what an interviewer wants to hear before the clever pass. For `n = 10⁵` (the constraint) O(n²) is ~10¹⁰ operations and will time out — so we present it, state the cost, and improve.

**Why it sets up Kadane's.** Notice the inner loop already maintains 'the sum of the subarray ending at `j` that started at `i`'. Kadane's insight is that we don't need to try every start `i` independently — we can decide, in one pass, whether to keep extending the current run or to abandon it. That observation collapses the outer loop entirely.
approaches.insight: The brute force already contains the seed of the optimal: a running sum extended one element at a time. The only wasteful part is restarting that sum from every possible left endpoint. The leap to O(n) is realising you can decide *on the fly* when restarting helps, instead of trying all restarts.

approaches.name: Kadane's Algorithm — One-Pass Running Sum (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'best subarray ending at each index' and explain the negative-prefix reset — don't just recite the two lines.
hints: Suppose you know the best subarray sum ending exactly at index i-1. How does that help you compute the best sum ending at index i?
At index i you either extend the previous run (cur + nums[i]) or start a brand-new run at nums[i]. Which would you pick, and when?
If the previous running sum is negative, it only drags nums[i] down — so reset. Keep cur = max(nums[i], cur + nums[i]) and track best = max(best, cur).
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single left-to-right pass doing O(1) work (two comparisons and an add) per element gives O(n) time, and we keep only two scalars (cur, best) so space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Walk the array once, maintaining `cur` = the largest sum of a subarray that *ends at the current index*, and `best` = the largest `cur` seen so far. At each element, `cur = max(num, cur + num)` and `best = max(best, cur)`.

**Why 'best ending here' is the right state.** Any maximum subarray has to end *somewhere*. If, for every index, we know the best subarray that ends exactly there, then the overall answer is just the maximum of those per-index bests. So we reduce a 2D search (start, end) to a 1D scan: only the end index moves, and `cur` summarises the best choice of start for that end.

**Why we reset when the prefix goes negative.** The choice `cur = max(num, cur + num)` says: either glue `num` onto the run ending at the previous index, or throw that run away and begin fresh at `num`. Starting fresh wins exactly when `cur + num < num`, i.e. when `cur < 0`. The reasoning is airtight — if the sum accumulated so far is negative, it can only *reduce* the total of anything we extend it into, so the optimal subarray ending here would never include that negative prefix. Drop it.

**Why `cur` and `best` are separate.** `cur` is allowed to fall (and reset) as we move right; it tracks a local, end-anchored quantity. `best` is the high-water mark that never decreases. Conflating them — for example returning `cur` at the end — would report the sum of the *last* run instead of the largest run anywhere.

**Why initialise to `nums[0]` and not 0.** The subarray must be non-empty, and an all-negative array's answer is its least-negative element. Seeding `cur = best = nums[0]` and scanning from index 1 guarantees we never invent an empty (sum-0) subarray.
approaches.insight: Kadane's is where DP and greedy shake hands. The DP view: `cur[i] = max(nums[i], cur[i-1] + nums[i])` is a one-line recurrence for 'best subarray ending at i'. The greedy view: at each step you make the locally optimal choice to discard a negative prefix, and you can *prove* that local choice is globally optimal because a negative prefix never helps. Most candidates memorise the two lines; saying *why the greedy discard is safe* is what lands the signal.

pitfalls: Seeding cur/best to 0 — returns 0 on all-negative input instead of the max element.
Returning cur instead of best — reports the last run, not the largest one.
Writing cur = cur + max(num, ...) or otherwise scrambling the max — the reset condition must compare num against cur + num.

commonMistakes: Initialising the running and best sums to 0, breaking all-negative inputs like [-3, -1, -2].
Returning the running sum cur instead of the high-water mark best.
Treating it as a subsequence problem and summing all positives — the subarray must be contiguous.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Zero-initialised sums on all-negative arrays
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Starting best at 0 means a fully-negative array reports 0, but the subarray must be non-empty, so the answer is the largest (least negative) element.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning cur instead of best
commonMistakesDetailed.why: cur is the best subarray ending at the LAST index; the global maximum may have occurred earlier and been lost when cur reset.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
cur = best = nums[0]
for num in nums[1:]:
    cur = max(num, cur + num)
    best = max(best, cur)
return cur  # wrong — ignores earlier peaks
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
cur = best = nums[0]
for num in nums[1:]:
    cur = max(num, cur + num)
    best = max(best, cur)
return best

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong reset comparison
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The reset must compare the bare element against the extended run. Reversing it (or adding before deciding) can keep a harmful negative prefix.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
cur = cur + nums[i];
if (cur < 0) cur = 0; // resets to 0, not nums[i] — drops a needed element

patternNote: Canonical Kadane's / 'best ending here' scan — keep a running value, reset it the moment a prefix stops helping, and remember the best ever seen. It's simultaneously a 1-line DP and a provable greedy; the same shape powers Maximum Product Subarray, Best Time to Buy/Sell Stock, and Maximum Sum Circular Subarray.
